passages.title: Visiting a Mangrove Forest
passages.text:
Last month, our class visited a mangrove forest near the coast. A narrow wooden path led from the entrance to a small viewing deck. On both sides, mangrove roots rose from the mud, and small crabs moved between them. The air smelled salty, and the water changed slowly as the tide came in.

A local guide explained that mangrove roots help hold the soil and provide shelter for young fish. We also learned that the forest can reduce the force of waves before they reach the shore. The guide asked us to observe quietly because loud sounds and careless movement could disturb birds and other animals.

Near the deck, there was a simple information board with pictures of common plants and animals. Students could write notes or sketch what they saw, but they were not allowed to collect shells, plants, or animals. A rubbish bin stood beside the exit, and visitors were asked to take their waste with them if the bin was full.

The visit was enjoyable because we could see the habitat while learning how to protect it. The guide reminded us that a mangrove forest is not just a place to visit; it is also a living environment that needs care.
hints: a narrow wooden path
roots help hold the soil
observe quietly

passages.title: How Our Town Recycles Waste
passages.text:
The town recycling center stands behind the public market, beside a small parking area. Its front room is bright and easy to enter, with large signs showing where different materials should go. Blue containers are used for paper, yellow ones for plastic bottles, and a separate cage holds clean metal cans. A weighing station stands near the back wall.

Residents can bring sorted materials from home twice a week. Staff members check the items before weighing them, because food, liquid, and mixed rubbish can make recycling more difficult. Materials that cannot be accepted are returned with a short explanation, so visitors can learn how to sort them correctly next time.

The center also has a small table where volunteers explain recycling to school groups. Students sometimes help make labels or record the amount of material collected. These activities do not replace the staff’s work, but they show how a community service operates.

The center is not a place where all waste disappears. Some materials still cannot be processed locally, and the center needs regular transport to send recyclable items to other facilities. Even so, it gives residents a practical way to reduce rubbish and understand what happens after they separate it at home.

passages.title: Joining a Neighborhood Clean-Up
passages.text:
Last Sunday, I joined a neighborhood clean-up with my cousin and several people from our street. We met near the community hall at seven in the morning. The organizer gave each group gloves, rubbish bags, and one area to clean. My group was responsible for the path beside a small stream.

At first, the work seemed easy. We collected plastic cups, snack wrappers, and dry leaves. Then we found a pile of rubbish behind a bush. Some bags were wet and heavy, so we asked an adult volunteer to help us move them safely. We did not touch broken glass with our hands; the volunteer used special tools to collect it.

After an hour, the path looked much cleaner. A few residents brought drinking water for the volunteers, and one shop owner lent us a large broom. We separated plastic bottles from other rubbish and placed the full bags at the collection point.

I went home tired but pleased. I had thought a clean-up was only about picking up rubbish, but I learned that planning, teamwork, and safe handling matter too. I also decided to carry a reusable bottle instead of buying a new plastic one every day.
hints: We met near the community hall

passages.title: Preparing for Our School Culture Day
passages.text:
Our class was responsible for a display about local traditions during the school culture day. For two weeks, we collected photographs, wrote short descriptions, and prepared a small table of traditional objects borrowed from families. We agreed that every object needed a label explaining its name and use.

The evening before the event, we discovered that several labels had been printed with the wrong names. Some students wanted to remove the objects and start again, but our teacher suggested checking each label against our notes first. Two classmates compared the photographs with the written descriptions, while the rest of us corrected the labels and printed replacements in the school office.

On the morning of the event, one family arrived late with a woven basket we had planned to display. We changed the order of the table so the other objects could be presented first. When the basket arrived, a student added its label and explained how it was used in daily life.

The display opened only a few minutes later than planned. Visitors asked questions, and some parents shared details we had not known. I learned that preparing a cultural event requires more than decorating a table. Accurate information, cooperation, and the ability to adjust plans are just as important.
hints: labels had been printed with the wrong names

passages.title: The Legend of Timun Mas
passages.text:
This retelling follows a familiar version of the Indonesian folktale Timun Mas. An elderly couple wished for a child. A giant named Buto Ijo gave them a cucumber seed, but he asked them to give him the child when she grew up. The couple agreed, hoping their wish would finally come true.

A golden cucumber later grew in their garden. Inside it, they found a baby girl and named her Timun Mas. They loved her and raised her carefully, but they worried as the day of Buto Ijo’s return came closer. Before the giant arrived, they gave Timun Mas several small packets and told her to run if she was in danger.

Timun Mas ran across fields and through the forest while Buto Ijo chased her. She threw the contents of the packets behind her. In this version, the objects became obstacles that slowed the giant, including thorny plants and deep mud. Each time he struggled to cross an obstacle, Timun Mas gained more time.

At last, she used the final packet, and the giant could not reach her. Timun Mas returned safely to the couple. The story is often understood as a tale about courage and quick thinking: she kept moving and used the help she had received instead of giving up.
hints: he asked them to give him the child

passages.title: The Legend of Lake Toba
passages.text:
This passage retells a familiar version of the Lake Toba legend from North Sumatra. A fisherman caught an unusual fish, which changed into a woman when he brought it home. They married, and she agreed to live with him after he promised never to reveal her unusual origin.

Years passed, and they had a son. The boy sometimes forgot his responsibilities. One day, his father asked him to bring food to the fields, but the boy delayed and ate some of it on the way. When the father discovered this, he became angry and called the boy the child of a fish. In doing so, he broke the promise he had made to his wife.

The woman was deeply hurt. She told her son to go to higher ground and then returned to the water. Dark clouds gathered, and heavy rain fell over the valley. In the legend, the water rose until it covered the area and formed Lake Toba. The land that remained in the middle became Samosir Island.

People tell different versions of the legend, but the broken promise is a key event in many retellings. The story can be understood as a warning about words spoken in anger and the importance of keeping promises. It is a cultural explanation connected to a landscape, not a scientific account of how the lake formed.
hints: promised never to reveal her unusual origin
he broke the promise
a cultural explanation connected to a landscape

passages.title: How to Make a Reusable Bag
passages.text:
You can make a simple reusable bag from an old T-shirt. It is a low-cost way to use clothing that you no longer wear. Choose a clean shirt that is still strong, and ask an adult for help if you need to use scissors.

First, lay the T-shirt flat on a table. Cut off the sleeves and cut around the neck to make a wide opening. Try to keep the cuts smooth so the top of the bag is comfortable to hold. Next, turn the shirt inside out and draw a straight line across the bottom, a few centimeters above the edge.

Cut short strips from the bottom edge up to the line. Tie each front strip to the matching strip at the back. Pull each knot gently to check that it is secure. When all the strips are tied, turn the shirt right side out again. The knots should now be inside the bag.

Finally, place a few light items inside and lift the bag carefully to test it. Do not use it for very heavy objects if the fabric or knots seem weak. Wash the bag when needed and let it dry fully before storing it. Reusing a shirt can reduce the need for a new bag, especially when you remember to bring it with you.
hints: lay the T-shirt flat
Tie each front strip to the matching strip at the back

passages.title: How to Reduce Waste at a School Event
passages.text:
A school event can be fun and exciting without creating a lot of waste. Follow these steps to help keep the event clean and environmentally friendly.

1. Plan and Set Goals. Discuss with your team how to reduce waste. Decide what items are really needed and set a clear goal, for example, to keep the event as close to zero waste as possible.

2. Choose Reusable Options. Use reusable plates, cups, and cutlery instead of single-use plastics. If possible, ask vendors, students, and guests to bring their own bottles and lunch containers.

3. Buy and Prepare Carefully. Estimate the right amount of food and materials. Avoid over-ordering so that unused items do not become waste. Choose suppliers who use minimal packaging or eco-friendly materials.

4. Set Up Waste Stations. Provide clearly labeled bins for different types of waste, such as recyclable, organic, and other waste. Use signs with pictures so everyone knows where to throw their trash.

5. Use Eco-Friendly Decorations. Choose decorations that can be reused, made from recycled materials, or are natural. Avoid balloons, plastic banners, and other items that often become litter.

6. Clean Up and Check the Results. After the event, separate the waste properly. Check how much waste was recycled or reused. Discuss what went well and what can be improved for the next event.
hints: set a clear goal
use reusable items
check the results after the event

passages.title: Why Students Should Learn Local Legends
passages.text:
Students should learn local legends because these stories connect people with the places and communities around them. A legend may explain how a place received its name, show which values a community respects, or preserve details about how people once understood the world. Discussing these stories can make cultural learning more concrete than memorizing a list of names.

Legends also provide useful reading practice. Students can identify characters, follow a sequence of events, compare different versions, and discuss the message of a story. When two versions differ, students can ask why a storyteller may have changed a detail. This encourages careful reading instead of assuming that every retelling is identical.

However, legends should not automatically be treated as verified history or scientific evidence. Teachers should explain the difference between a traditional story, a historical record, and a scientific explanation. Some students may also feel that a legend is not connected to their own family background. Lessons can respond by including stories from different regions and inviting students to research them respectfully.

For these reasons, local legends deserve a place in learning when they are taught thoughtfully. They can support language skills and cultural understanding, provided that students are encouraged to ask questions and recognize the difference between storytelling and evidence.
hints: connect people with the places and communities
compare different versions
difference between storytelling and evidence

passages.title: Is It Better to Visit Tourist Places on Weekdays?
passages.text:
Visiting tourist places on weekdays can be a good choice, but it is not always best for every traveler. On many weekdays, popular sites are less crowded than they are on weekends. Visitors may spend less time waiting, hear guides more clearly, and take photographs without blocking other people. A quieter visit can also make it easier to notice details in a museum, park, or historic area.

Weekday travel may help local businesses too, especially when visitors come during periods that are usually quiet. However, the benefit depends on the place and the season. Some shops or food stalls may open for fewer hours on weekdays, and certain attractions may have limited activities when school groups are not visiting.

Schedules are another important factor. Students and workers may not be able to travel on a weekday without missing school or taking leave. Weekend visits can be more practical for families who need to travel together. Weather, transport schedules, ticket prices, and the opening hours of the attraction can matter more than the day itself.

Therefore, travelers should compare the conditions rather than assume weekdays are always better. Weekdays can offer a calmer experience, while weekends may provide more convenient schedules or a livelier atmosphere. The best choice depends on the visitor’s needs and the specific destination.
hints: less crowded than they are on weekends
the benefit depends on the place and the season
compare the conditions
